claim: Life relies on the interplay between catalytic activity and information processing carried out by biological polymers.
source: Life as we know it relies on the interplay between catalytic activity and information processing carried out by biological polymers.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the fundamental characteristics of life.

claim: Non-catalyzed spontaneous cleavage promotes proliferation by generating short fragments that act as primers in a system capable of non-enzymatic templated replication.
source: Starting with a system capable of non-enzymatic templated replication, we demonstrate that even non-catalyzed spontaneous cleavage would promote proliferation by generating short fragments that act as primers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical model and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Catalytic cleavage function can naturally emerge and proliferate in a system of non-enzymatic templated replication.
source: Furthermore, we show that catalytic cleavage function can naturally emerge and proliferate in this system.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the mathematical model and numerical simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: A cooperative catalytic network with four subpopulations of oligomers is selected by evolution in competition with chains lacking catalytic activity.
source: Specifically, a cooperative catalytic network with four subpopulations of oligomers is selected by the evolution in competition with chains lacking catalytic activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the model analysis and phase portraits shown in the manuscript.

claim: The cooperative system emerges through functional differentiation of oligomers into catalysts and their substrates.
source: The cooperative system emerges through the functional differentiation of oligomers into catalysts and their substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model structure and dynamics.

claim: The model is inspired by the structure of the hammerhead RNA enzyme and other DNA- and RNA-based enzymes with cleavage activity.
source: The model is inspired by the structure of the hammerhead RNA enzyme as well as other DNA- and RNA-based enzymes with cleavage activity that readily emerge through natural or artificial selection.
evidence: This references existing knowledge about ribozymes and DNA enzymes.

claim: The emergence of the cooperative catalytic network requires the catalytic rate enhancement over the spontaneous cleavage rate to be at least 10²–10³.
source: In particular, we show that it requires the catalytic rate enhancement over the spontaneous cleavage rate to be at least 102–103, a factor consistent with the existing experiments.
evidence: This is derived from the model analysis and compared with experimental data.

claim: Evolutionary pressure leads to a further increase in catalytic efficiency.
source: The evolutionary pressure leads to a further increase in catalytic efficiency.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the fitness landscape analysis in the model.

claim: The RNA world theory is a promising hypothesis for the origin of life.
source: One promising hypothesis is the RNA world theory (Gilbert, 1986; Doudna and Szostak, 1989; Orgel, 2004; Lincoln and Joyce, 2009; Robertson and Joyce, 2012; Higgs and Lehman, 2015), inspired by the discovery of ribozymes (Kruger et al., 1982), that is, RNA molecules capable of enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple scientific publications.

claim: According to the RNA world hypothesis, all processes in early life were carried out by RNA, which was used both to store information and catalyze biochemical reactions.
source: According to this hypothesis, all processes in early life were carried out by the RNA, which was used both to store information and catalyze biochemical reactions.
evidence: This is a description of the RNA world hypothesis from the scientific literature.

claim: Specific ribozymes capable of catalyzing self-replication of arbitrary RNA sequences require rather long and carefully designed RNA sequences that are highly unlikely to arise spontaneously.
source: However, based on the results of the existing experiments (Bartel and Szostak, 1993; Horning and Joyce, 2016), such a catalytic function requires rather long and carefully designed RNA sequences, which are highly unlikely to arise spontaneously.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: One of the simplest catalytic activities of ribozymes is their ability to cleave an RNA sequence at a specific site.
source: In contrast, one of the simplest catalytic activities of ribozymes is their ability to cleave an RNA sequence at a specific site.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribozyme functions.

claim: Ribozymes with cleavage activity independently evolved in multiple branches of life.
source: Indeed, such ribozymes independently evolved in multiple branches of life (de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010) and have been shown to emerge rapidly and repeatedly from artificial selection (Williams et al., 1995; Salehi-Ashtiani and Szostak, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific publications.

claim: DNA molecules are capable of site-specific cleavage targeting either RNA or DNA sequences.
source: DNA molecules have also been shown to be capable of site-specific cleavage targeting either RNA (Breaker and Joyce, 1994) or DNA sequences (Silverman, 2005; Chandra et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Non-enzymatic templated replication can lead to the formation of longer chains.
source: In a series of previous studies, we have shown that non-enzymatic templated replication can lead to the formation of longer chains (Tkachenko and Maslov, 2015) as well as to a reduction in sequence entropy (Tkachenko and Maslov, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Non-enzymatic templated replication can lead to a reduction in sequence entropy.
source: In a series of previous studies, we have shown that non-enzymatic templated replication can lead to the formation of longer chains (Tkachenko and Maslov, 2015) as well as to a reduction in sequence entropy (Tkachenko and Maslov, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Reduction in sequence entropy through templated ligation has been observed experimentally for DNA oligomers.
source: Such a reduction in entropy has subsequently been observed experimentally for templated ligation of DNA oligomers (Kudella et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The breakup of chains creates a new pair of potential primers that could be elongated during subsequent nights.
source: The key observation behind our model is that the breakup (cleavage) of a chain creates a new pair of potential primers. Each of them could be elongated during subsequent nights.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model structure.

claim: Breakup of chains results in their proliferation.
source: Thus, somewhat counterintuitively, breakup of chains results in their proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: Templated-assisted replication of heteropolymers has a generic tendency to substantially reduce their sequence entropy.
source: Our previous theoretical (Tkachenko and Maslov, 2015; Tkachenko and Maslov, 2018) and experimental (Kudella et al., 2021) results demonstrated that templated-assisted replication of heteropolymers has a generic tendency to substantially reduce their sequence entropy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Reduction in sequence entropy significantly increases the likelihood of end-to-middle hybridization of chains during the night phase.
source: Such reduction has important consequences in the context of the current work: it significantly increases the likelihood of end-to-middle hybridization of chains during the night phase.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the properties of the system.

claim: The ability of a heteropolymer to catalyze cleavage would be selected by evolution.
source: It is therefore reasonable to expect that the ability of a heteropolymer to catalyze cleavage would be selected by the evolution.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the model showing that cleavage promotes proliferation.

claim: Some of the simplest known RNA-based enzymes (ribozymes) have cleavage function.
source: Incidentally, some of the simplest known RNA-based enzymes (ribozymes) have exactly this function (Kruger et al., 1982; Prody et al., 1986; Hutchins et al., 1986; Scott et al., 1995; Williams et al., 1995; Salehi-Ashtiani and Szostak, 2001; de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010; Scott et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to scientific literature.

claim: The minimal structure of the hammerhead ribozyme consists of a core region of 15 (mostly) invariant nucleotides flanked by three helical stems formed by mutually complementary RNA sequences.
source: The minimal structure of the hammerhead ribozyme (Pley et al., 1994; Scott et al., 1995; Scott et al., 2013) consists of a core region of 15 (mostly) invariant nucleotides flanked by three helical stems formed by mutually complementary RNA sequences.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of the hammerhead ribozyme.

claim: The cleavage in hammerhead ribozyme happens at a specific site located immediately adjacent to one of the helical stems.
source: The cleavage happens at a specific site of this structure, located immediately adjacent to one of these stems.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hammerhead ribozyme structure and function.

claim: Two-chain hammerhead ribozyme structures are realized in certain DNA-cleaving DNA enzymes.
source: Furthermore, such two-chain structuresare realized in certain DNA-cleaving DNA enzymes (Chandra et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Template poisoning has only a moderate effect if the night phase is not too long.
source: This indicates that template poisoning has only a moderate effect if the night phase is not too long.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the binding kinetics analysis presented in Appendix 1.

claim: The cooperative fixed point is mainly maintained by catalytic cleavage.
source: This fixed point is mainly maintained by catalytic cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the model structure and parameter values.

claim: Once the cooperative state emerges, it drives out all chain sequences that still rely on non-catalytic cleavage for replication.
source: Thus, once the cooperative state emerges, it drives out all chain sequences that still rely on non-catalytic cleavage for replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the competitive dynamics based on monomer concentration.

claim: The non-cooperative solution has a fitness of 1, while the cooperative solution has a fitness higher than 2.
source: Note that the non-cooperative solution has a fitness of 1, while the cooperative solution has a fitness higher than 2.
evidence: This is calculated from the model using the fitness definition m*/m*_coop.

claim: For a fixed value of λ, the selective pressure would drive β down to the lower boundary separating cooperative and non-cooperative regions.
source: In other words, for a given λ, the selective pressure would drive β down to the lower boundary separating cooperative and non-cooperative regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the fitness landscape analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: λ and β are expected to co-evolve together.
source: However, λ and β are expected to co-evolve together.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the structural relationship between these parameters.

claim: As a consequence of selective pressure, both λ and β are expected to increase in the course of evolution driving the system up the ridge in Figure 4.
source: As a consequence of the selective pressure, both λ and β are expected to increase in the course of the evolution driving the system up the ridge in Figure 4.
evidence: This is supported by the fitness landscape analysis and Monte Carlo simulations.

claim: The cooperative steady state emerges when the catalytic rate enhancement over the spontaneous cleavage rate is at least 10²–10³.
source: Our results indicate that the cooperative steady state emerges when the catalytic rate enhancement over the spontaneous cleavage rate is at least 102–103.
evidence: This is derived from the model analysis.

claim: The catalytic rate enhancement of 10²–10³ is relatively modest compared to the 10⁹ enhancement reported for a highly optimized hammerhead ribozyme.
source: This is a relatively modest gain compared to the 109 enhancement reported for a highly optimized hammerhead ribozyme Scott et al., 2013.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited experimental data.

claim: The catalytic rate enhancement of 10²–10³ is comparable to the rate enhancement observed after only five rounds of in vitro selection from an unbiased sample of random RNA sequences.
source: However, it is comparable to the rate enhancement observed after only five rounds of in vitro selection from an unbiased sample of random RNA sequences (Salehi-Ashtiani and Szostak, 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited experimental data.

claim: The VCG model is based on the observation that a relatively long ancestral genome can be stored as a collection of short overlapping RNA fragments of a circular master sequence or its complement.
source: It is based on the observation that a relatively long ancestral genome can be stored as a collection of short overlapping RNA fragments of a circular master sequence or its complement.
evidence: This is a description of the VCG model from the cited literature.

claim: The VCG model assumes unidirectional non-enzymatic replication of fragments.
source: The model assumes unidirectional non-enzymatic replication of these fragments.
evidence: This is a description of the VCG model from the cited literature.

claim: The VCG is susceptible to sequence scrambling, where the appearance of repeats in the master sequence results in the loss of integrity of an entire circular genome.
source: On the other hand, computer simulations indicate that the VCG is susceptible to so-called sequence scrambling, where the appearance of repeats in the master sequence results in the loss of integrity of an entire circular genome (Chamanian and Higgs, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to computational studies.

claim: The presented model assumes that non-enzymatic templated polymerization is bidirectional.
source: Our model, while sharing some elements with the VCG model, differs in two important aspects: (i) it assumes that the non-enzymatic templated polymerization is bidirectional, and (ii) the functional activity of the heteropolymer is localized in a relatively short sequence region that is catalytically cleaved and thus replicated first.
evidence: This is a description of a key assumption of the model.

claim: In the presented model, the functional activity of the heteropolymer is localized in a relatively short sequence region that is catalytically cleaved and thus replicated first.
source: Our model, while sharing some elements with the VCG model, differs in two important aspects: (i) it assumes that the non-enzymatic templated polymerization is bidirectional, and (ii) the functional activity of the heteropolymer is localized in a relatively short sequence region that is catalytically cleaved and thus replicated first.
evidence: This is a description of a key feature of the model.

claim: Possible scrambling outside of the narrow functional region does not affect the viability of the autocatalytic system.
source: This implies that possible scrambling outside of the narrow functional region does not affect the viability of our autocatalytic system.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model structure.

claim: RNA or DNA can be used as model polymers in experiments to verify the main conclusions, as both have demonstrated catalytic abilities in cleavage reactions.
source: RNA or DNA can be used as model polymers in such experiments, as both have demonstrated catalytic abilities in cleavage reactions (de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010; Williams et al., 1995; Salehi-Ashtiani and Szostak, 2001; Breaker and Joyce, 1994; Silverman, 2005; Chandra et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model assumes polymerization in both the 5′-to-3′ and 3′-to-5′ directions, unlike traditional PCR which only adds new nucleotides in the 5′-to-3′ direction.
source: However, it is important to note that our model assumes polymerization in both the 5′-to-3′ and 3′-to-5′ directions, unlike traditional PCR, which only adds new nucleotides in the 5′-to-3′ direction.
evidence: This is a comparison between the model assumptions and known biochemical processes.

claim: The problem of bidirectional polymerization was solved by evolution using Okazaki fragments.
source: This problem of bidirectional polymerization was solved by evolution using Okazaki fragments (Okazaki et al., 1968).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the discovery of Okazaki fragments.

claim: A stable cooperative solution can be achieved with as few as four subpopulations of chains.
source: Our study shows that a stable cooperative solution can be achieved with as few as four subpopulations of chains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model analysis.

claim: There is a wide range of conditions under which the catalytic network proliferates and significantly outcompetes non-catalytic ancestors of the constituent chains.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that there is a wide range of conditions under which this catalytic network proliferates and significantly outcompetes non-catalytic ancestors of the constituent chains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase diagram and fitness landscape analysis.

claim: A faster, catalyzed cleavage would be selected by evolution.
source: This suggests that a faster, catalyzed cleavage would be selected by the evolution.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model showing that cleavage promotes replication.

claim: DNA or RNA sequences capable of catalyzing site-specific cleavage are relatively simple and readily arise via either natural or artificial selection.
source: Furthermore, DNA or RNA sequences capable of catalyzing site-specific cleavage are known to be relatively simple and readily arise via either natural or artificial selection (de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010; Williams et al., 1995; Salehi-Ashtiani and Szostak, 2001; Breaker and Joyce, 1994; Silverman, 2005; Chandra et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.
